results.content: When to build a Docker image. Docker is an open source project that builds on many long familiar technologies from operating systems research: LXC containers, virtualization of the OS, and a hash-based or git-like versioning and differencing system, among others. With a Docker image, we can quickly spin up containers with the same configuration. We can then share these images with our team, so we will all be running containers which all have the same configuration. There are several ways to create Docker images, but the best way is to create a `Dockerfile` and use the `docker build` command. The above command will spin up a new container based on our image and run it. Many images require some extra parameters to be passed to the run command, so take some time to read through the documentation of an image before you use it. results.title: Gregory Szorc's Digital Home | Deterministic and Minimal Docker Images
results.content: ## Deterministic and Minimal Docker Images. But one supposedly solved part of Docker still bothers me: image creation. I dare say Docker has solved the image *distribution* problem. This non-determinism of building Docker images really bothers me. There are many people who are justifiably paranoid about running binaries produced by others and pre-built Docker images set off all kinds of alarms. Determinism and verifiability as part of Docker image creation help solve this problem. So much for Docker image distribution. Do I really need a package manager in my Docker image? As a security-minded person, I want my Docker images to consist of only the files they need, especially binary files. When you factor in that Docker image creation isn't deterministic, you also realize that different people are producing different versions of images from the same Dockerfiles and that you have to spend extra bandwidth transferring the different versions around. I understand why Docker images are neither deterministic nor minimal: making them so is a hard problem. I would absolutely love if more and more Docker images were the result of a deterministic build process like Nix. Perhaps you could define the full set of packages (with versions) that would be used. Then, create an archive of that environment and pipe it into *docker build* to create a minimal Docker image. Tools like makejail pair down the produced packages into something minimal, which you then turn into your Docker image. Regular people can still pull binary images, but they are much smaller and more in tune with Docker's principles of minimalism. You really want a recipe that knows how to create a set of relevant files and some metadata like what ports to expose, what command to run on container start, etc and turn that into your Docker image. I'm pretty sure of what it would take to add deterministic and verifiable building of minimal and more secure Docker images. And, if someone solved this problem, it could be applicable outside of Docker (again, Docker images are essentially chroot environments plus metadata). I hope the Docker community latches on to these ideas and makes deterministic, verifiable, and minimal images the default, not the exception.
